analysis.one_liner: Taxes carbon emissions to fund highways, coastal protection, and aid for low-income households, while repealing the gas tax and pausing climate rules.
analysis.headline: The first Republican-sponsored carbon tax bill in a decade, introduced July 23, 2018 with 2 cosponsors, was referred to seven House committees and never received a single markup or vote before Congress ended January 3, 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would put a price on the carbon pollution released by coal, oil, and natural gas, starting at $24 per ton in 2020 and rising every year, with automatic $2-per-ton increases if emissions miss set targets. The money would flow into a new trust fund, mostly for highway and aviation infrastructure, plus grants to low-income households, protection against coastal flooding, and retraining for displaced energy workers. In exchange, it would repeal the federal gasoline and aviation fuel taxes and stop the EPA from writing or enforcing new greenhouse gas rules under the Clean Air Act until 2033 or until emissions targets are met.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers and travelers benefit from roughly $75 billion a year in sustained highway and aviation funding paid for by the carbon tax instead of the gas tax. Low-income households (those on SNAP, SSI, or below 150 percent of the poverty line) would get monthly state-distributed grants. Coastal communities facing chronic flooding would get a new grant program, and energy workers displaced by the transition would get a decade of retraining, relocation, early-retirement, and health benefits. U.S. manufacturers in energy-intensive sectors would be shielded from foreign competition through a border tax that applies the same carbon cost to imports.

how_it_helps.text: Imposes an escalating economy-wide tax on greenhouse gas emissions from fossil fuels, industrial processes, and certain products, starting at $24 per metric ton of CO2-equivalent in 2020 and rising by 2 percentage points plus inflation each year, with an additional $2 per ton if cumulative emissions exceed scheduled levels.

Dedicates 75 percent of the carbon tax revenue to a new trust fund, of which 70 percent goes to the Highway Trust Fund and 2.5 percent to the Airport and Airway Trust Fund, replacing the gas tax revenue that would be repealed.

Directs 10 percent of the trust fund to monthly state grants that must be distributed to eligible low-income households, including households receiving SNAP benefits, Medicare Part D low-income subsidies, or SSI, or earning up to 150 percent of the poverty line.

Creates a grant program for coastal flooding mitigation and adaptation projects such as living shorelines, drainage improvements, and microgrids, prioritizing special flood hazard areas and critical infrastructure.
Funds a 10-year program of retraining, relocation expenses, early retirement, and health benefits for energy-sector workers displaced by the carbon tax.
Applies a border tax adjustment so imported energy-intensive goods pay the same carbon cost as domestic goods, and domestic exporters get rebates, to prevent factories from simply moving overseas.

analysis.who_pays: Anyone who buys gasoline, diesel, natural gas, coal-fired electricity, or carbon-intensive goods would pay more as producers pass the tax through at the mine, refinery, and plant gate. The bill's household relief is limited: only 10 percent of the trust fund goes to low-income grants, so middle-income households would absorb higher energy and goods prices with no direct offset. The EPA's authority to write and enforce new greenhouse gas rules for fuels and industrial sources would be suspended, so if a future Congress repealed the tax, the regulatory backstop would already be gone.

drawbacks.text: Energy costs rise for all households and businesses, and the low-income relief is comparatively small: only 10 percent of the trust fund is set aside for household grants, and just 1.5 percent for home weatherization, leaving middle-income households with no direct offset for higher fuel and utility prices.

The bill suspends EPA greenhouse gas rulemaking and enforcement under the Clean Air Act for fuels and taxed industrial emissions until January 1, 2033, trading binding regulation for a tax; if a future Congress repealed the tax, the regulatory limit on emissions would already have been given up.

The National Climate Commission it creates is authorized to accept private-sector donations as its funding, with only public disclosure of amounts and sources as a safeguard against industry influence over its review of climate policy.

The border tax adjustment gives the President discretion to waive it for any sector or product deemed not in the national interest, leaving a core protection for domestic manufacturers subject to unilateral executive override.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This is a genuine, if compromise-shaped, climate policy: a rising economy-wide carbon price with real money for infrastructure, coastal protection, and worker transition, paired with automatic penalties if emissions targets are missed. But its design favors industry and drivers over households: unlike full per-capita dividend proposals, only about 7.5 percent of total revenue reaches low-income households, most consumers would pay the tax at the pump and on their utility bills without an offset, and the price paid for industry buy-in is a decade-long suspension of Clean Air Act enforcement. It is defensible climate legislation with a real regressivity problem and a regulatory trade-off an honest supporter has to acknowledge.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to seven House committees on the day it was introduced and to several subcommittees afterward, but no committee ever held a markup and the House never voted on it before the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Carlos Curbelo, a Florida Republican, introduced the bill on July 23, 2018, with Representative Brian Fitzpatrick as cosponsor.

The bill was referred the same day to seven full committees, including Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, and Transportation and Infrastructure, and in the following weeks to subcommittees on aviation, highways, water resources, environment, energy and mineral resources, and commodity exchanges.
No committee reported the bill, no markup was held, and no floor vote ever occurred before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because it died without any committee action, fossil fuel producers and other emitters avoided a new carbon tax, and the status quo of the existing gas tax and existing EPA rules simply continued. Drivers saw no change at the pump from this bill, and no low-income grants or coastal protection funding were ever created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Emitters avoided the carbon tax entirely

for.name: Rep. Carlos Curbelo
for.what_they_did: Introduced the MARKET CHOICE Act on July 23, 2018, the first carbon tax bill from a House Republican in roughly a decade.

for.name: Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as its only named cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: Rep. Kevin Brady
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on July 23, 2018; the committee took no further action, holding no markup, before the Congress ended.

against.name: House Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, Natural Resources, Transportation and Infrastructure, Science, Education and the Workforce, and Agriculture Committees
against.what_they_did: Split jurisdiction across seven committees, none of which reported the bill or scheduled it for a vote in the five-plus months remaining in the session.

against.name: Americans for Prosperity and allied anti-tax groups
against.role: Outside conservative organizations opposing carbon taxation
against.what_they_did: Ran public campaigns urging lawmakers to reject any carbon tax, part of the broader political climate in which no House Republican leadership effort advanced the bill.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so no roll-call split exists; the sponsor and both cosponsors were Republicans, no Democrat signed on, and the Republican majority never moved the bill out of committee.

industries.industry: Coal, oil, and natural gas producers
industries.note: They would pay the new tax at the mine mouth, refinery exit, or gas plant exit, but in exchange the bill suspends EPA greenhouse gas rulemaking and enforcement for fuels and taxed industrial emissions until 2033, giving them a new tax in return for a decade of regulatory relief. Consumers would pay most of the tax through higher fuel prices.

Seventy percent of the trust fund goes to the Highway Trust Fund and 2.5 percent to aviation, a sustained funding stream replacing the repealed gas tax; the same money finances roads that drivers use.

Their process emissions are taxed, but a border tax adjustment taxes competing imports at the same rate and rebates the tax on exports, shielding them from competitors in countries without carbon pricing.

Fossil-fired generation bears the fuel-based carbon tax, which raises electricity costs for customers; the bill offers utilities no dividend mechanism, though the fuel regulatory moratorium removes a compliance threat.
The federal aviation fuel excise tax is repealed, but jet fuel still bears the carbon tax, and the Airport and Airway Trust Fund is kept solvent with a 2.5 percent share of carbon revenue.
